questions.question: Write balanced equations for the reactions of dilute HCl with: (a) zinc metal, (b) calcium carbonate, (c) copper(II) oxide.
questions.answer: (a) Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑. (b) 2 HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. (c) 2 HCl + CuO → CuCl₂ + H₂O. All three illustrate acid + (metal / carbonate / metal oxide) → products including salt.
questions.explanation: Three classic reactions of an acid.

questions.question: Distinguish between (i) acid and base, (ii) strong and weak acid, (iii) concentrated and dilute solution.
questions.answer: (i) An ACID releases H⁺ ions in water and turns blue litmus red; a BASE releases OH⁻ ions in water and turns red litmus blue. (ii) STRONG acid ionises COMPLETELY in water (HCl, H₂SO₄); WEAK acid ionises PARTIALLY (CH₃COOH, citric). (iii) CONCENTRATED solution has a LARGE amount of solute per litre; DILUTE solution has a SMALL amount per litre. 'Strong/weak' is about ionisation; 'concentrated/dilute' is about amount.

questions.question: Why do we always add ACID to WATER and never the reverse? What happens if we do it wrong?
questions.answer: Diluting a concentrated acid is highly EXOTHERMIC — heat is released as ions hydrate. If water is added to concentrated acid, the small amount of water heats up rapidly to boiling and may cause the acid to SPLASH OUT, possibly causing burns. By adding acid slowly to a much LARGER volume of water, the heat is dispersed safely. Always wear safety goggles too.

questions.question: Order these by INCREASING acidity: stomach acid (pH 1.5), pure water (pH 7), milk (pH 6.5), seawater (pH 8), lemon juice (pH 2).
questions.answer: Order from MOST BASIC to MOST ACIDIC (increasing acidity = decreasing pH): seawater (pH 8) → pure water (pH 7) → milk (pH 6.5) → lemon juice (pH 2) → stomach acid (pH 1.5). Stomach acid is the most acidic; seawater is the most basic of this list.

questions.question: How does an antacid work? Give a chemical example.
questions.answer: Indigestion is caused by EXCESS HCl (stomach acid). An ANTACID is a mild base that NEUTRALISES the excess acid. Common chemical antacids: magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia, Mg(OH)₂) or sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO₃). Reaction: HCl + NaHCO₃ → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂↑. The CO₂ is released as a burp; the salt and water are harmless.

questions.question: Write the chemical formula and ONE major use each of: baking soda, washing soda, plaster of Paris.
questions.answer: Baking soda: NaHCO₃ — used in baking (releases CO₂ on heating, makes cakes rise) and as a mild antacid. Washing soda: Na₂CO₃·10 H₂O — used in detergents to soften hard water and in glass-making. Plaster of Paris: CaSO₄·½ H₂O — used in hospitals for casts to support broken bones, and in decorative plaster work.

questions.question: Describe the chlor-alkali process. What are its three useful products and one use of each?
questions.answer: Process: ELECTROLYSIS of brine (concentrated aqueous NaCl). Equation: 2 NaCl(aq) + 2 H₂O(l) → 2 NaOH(aq) + Cl₂(g)↑ + H₂(g)↑. Three useful products: (1) Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) — soap making. (2) Chlorine (Cl₂) — disinfection of water, PVC manufacture. (3) Hydrogen (H₂) — fuel, ammonia synthesis (fertilisers).

questions.question: A student adds dilute hydrochloric acid to four substances: (a) sodium carbonate, (b) zinc granules, (c) copper turnings, (d) copper(II) oxide. For each, predict whether a reaction occurs and write the balanced equation. State an observation that indicates the reaction has happened.
questions.answer: (a) Sodium carbonate Na₂CO₃: reacts vigorously. 2 HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2 NaCl + H₂O + CO₂↑. Observation: rapid effervescence; gas turns lime water milky. (b) Zinc Zn: reacts. Zn + 2 HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑. Observation: bubbles of colourless gas (H₂); burns with a 'pop'. (c) Copper Cu: NO reaction with dilute HCl — copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. (d) Copper(II) oxide CuO: reacts. 2 HCl + CuO → CuCl₂ + H₂O. Observation: black CuO dissolves to form a blue-green solution of CuCl₂.
questions.explanation: Four reactions; identifies which work + observation each.

questions.question: Explain why pH is important in (i) the human stomach, (ii) tooth decay, and (iii) plant growth in soil. For each, give a real-life consequence and a way to manage it.
questions.answer: (i) STOMACH: pH ≈ 1.5-3 due to HCl, which kills bacteria and helps digest proteins. Excess acid causes acidity / heartburn. Manage with antacids (Mg(OH)₂, NaHCO₃) which neutralise extra acid. (ii) TOOTH DECAY: bacteria in the mouth ferment sugars to acids. When pH drops below 5.5, tooth enamel (calcium phosphate) starts to dissolve. Manage by brushing with basic toothpastes (which contain mild bases) and cutting down on sugar. (iii) PLANT GROWTH: most plants grow best in soil with pH between 6 and 7.5. Very acidic soil (pH < 5) hurts crops; very alkaline soil (pH > 8) also hurts. Manage acidic soil by adding LIME (CaO or Ca(OH)₂); manage alkaline soil by adding gypsum or organic compost.

questions.question: Common salt (NaCl) is the raw material for several industrial chemicals. Name FOUR products that can be made from common salt and the reactions involved. Mention one use of each product.
questions.answer: (1) Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) — by electrolysis of brine: 2 NaCl + 2 H₂O → 2 NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂. Use: soap making. (2) Chlorine (Cl₂) — same chlor-alkali process. Use: PVC, disinfectants, water treatment. (3) Bleaching powder (CaOCl₂) — Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O. Use: bleaching cotton / paper, disinfection of drinking water. (4) Baking soda (NaHCO₃) — by Solvay-style process: NaCl + H₂O + NH₃ + CO₂ → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl. Use: baking, antacid, fire extinguishers. (Bonus 5) Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10 H₂O) — formed from baking soda by heating then re-crystallising. Use: detergents, glass-making.
questions.explanation: Common salt → four products + reactions + uses.
